cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Approve the Cover Story
cards.instruction: Get someone to endorse an explanation that protects the plan, reputation, or people involved.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I'll decide how we handle this. Can you approve 'delivery delay' in the newsletter? I don't want our new volunteer blamed for the melted cake.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: She delivered it on time. We left it by the radiator.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You can question the details after my decision. Then 'storage problem'. Will you approve that?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Only if we mention the refund.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Absolutely. 'Storage problem; full refund arranged.' Can I put your name under it?

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 and A3 ask B to approve, and A5 seeks B's name; the higher-status claim is not sustained in that permission relationship.

relationship.evidence: B2 protects factual accuracy and B4 insists on remedy information, not just flattery.

heightening.evidence: A5 secures a more defensible shared statement after B4 condition.

specificity.evidence: A1 newsletter and melted cake establish the reputational task and person protected.
